newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing debt market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing debt market report.

text.p: Dutch bonds ended higher on Wednesday, back close to two-month peaks after surprisingly weak U.S inflation data boosted Europe, but the local market remained bedevilled by very low turnover, dealers said.
Guilders rallied with Bunds after a drop of 0.6 percent in the April U.S. producer price index -- the biggest fall since August 1993 -- after standing mixed and nearly motionless for most of the day.
The slightly heavy Dutch market again underperformed Germany on the way up, though, with the 10-year yield discount shaving another two basis points after narrowing on Tuesday.
The upmove was not paired with any significant cash trade, dealers said, with investors uninterested at current levels.
"Interest rates are low and seen rising," one said. "In that environment it is just too expensive at the moment. There are no buyers and probably won't be until we see higher yields."

A yield level of six percent on the 10-year benchmark would likely mark the point where institutions might return, he said. The 5.75 percent February 2007 issue settled with a yield of 5.57 percent on Wednesday.
The market shrugged off news on the Dutch state's 1997 funding requirements.
The finance ministry's capital markets agency said on Wednesday that 10 billion guilders of its 1997 borrowing requirement still remained to be raised.
The agency also said in its spring memorandum that the forecast 1997 Dutch budget deficit had been cut to 18.6 billion guilders from a previously estimated 21 billion.
"It was already pretty much discounted in the market, although 10 billion seems a little low to me," a broker said.
"It is pretty sad for the liquidity of the Dutch market."
Dealers said the tight supply situation has been driving big players to switch into Germany.
"The less supply there is here, the more the institutions are going to buy Bunds," one said. "It may get even quieter over here." -- Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000, Fax +31 20 504 5040
